title: The signature and the thing it stands for
task: Separate what is asserted from what is supported
scene: Records custodian Nell Achterberg opens the Ward file on the hall's long table. The cover says seven years served of fourteen. Every page is signed. The unit has fifteen working days, and this morning buys only three checks.
question: Verify what the morning allows, and hold whatever the store cannot stand behind.
takeaway: A record is evidence that a claim was accepted, which is not evidence for the claim.
why: A file compresses months of work into signed claims. A signature shows who accepted a claim, not whether the condition was true. That difference matters most for claims carrying the case. Distance and lighting are both decisive and neither has a repeatable measurement behind it. The certainty statement is different: it is a real record, but its date changes what it can support. With only three checks, verification belongs where an unsupported claim could change the review.
assumes: a signature records that somebody accepted a claim at the time
a review has less time than a file has pages
answerText: Hold the distance and the lighting. Both decide what could have been seen, both rest on a phrase rather than a measurement, and neither has anything in the store behind it. The certainty statement is a real signed document — what is wrong with it is its date, which is a different objection.

title: Six at once
task: Establish what Cardoza was actually asked to do
scene: Marcus Ilori has the 4 December 2019 array record on the table. Six photographs were laid out together. The witness was asked whether the man she saw was among them. It was standard procedure that year.
question: What does laying all six photographs out together invite a witness to do?
takeaway: Shown together, a lineup asks which face is closest; shown one at a time, it asks whether this is the face.
why: Six faces shown together invite relative judgment. The witness can ask which face is closest to memory instead of whether any face is the offender. That easier question always has a winner, even when the offender is absent. Nothing dishonest has to happen for the error to appear. Sequential presentation changes the task. Each face must be judged before the next arrives, which makes rejecting the lineup a live response rather than a comparison lost among six alternatives.
assumes: a lineup contains one suspect and a number of people known not to be the offender

choices: Compare them and choose whichever is nearest her memory
Report a lower level of certainty than she actually holds
Rely on colour and complexion detail the scene could not have given her
Recall the array afterwards in place of recalling the man in the doorway
rebuttals: Certainty tends to rise after a choice from an array rather than fall, so this is the wrong direction.
Complexion is a real limit of that night, and it constrains what she saw before the array existed.
Remembering the array instead of the event is a later problem, and it needs a second procedure to appear.

title: What a clean file would look like
task: Guard the review against the answer it wants
scene: Grace Ntuli stops the first meeting four minutes in. Everybody in the room came here to find bad procedure, she says, and the file has not been opened yet. She wants something written on the whiteboard before it is.
question: What does writing down the features of a sound 2019 procedure protect the review from?
takeaway: Write down what would count against you before you look, or you will not recognise it later.
why: Expectancy changes what people notice and remember without making them fabricate evidence. Reviewers who expect bad procedure naturally recognize faults faster than facts pointing the other way. Writing the standard first creates a comparison instead of a search. The same logic supports preregistration in experiments. Evidence that contradicts the room's expectation already has a place to land. That makes it harder to move the standard after the file starts telling a persuasive story.
assumes: people find more of what they are looking for than of what they are not

choices: Counting only the findings that point the way the room already leans
The board rejecting a report that has not been agreed in advance
Disagreement between the psychologists and the lawyers about the standard
Spending time on documents that turn out not to matter to the outcome
rebuttals: The board's agreement is not what is at issue; it reads the report after the work rather than before it.
A shared standard does help the two professions agree, and that is a benefit rather than the risk being guarded against.
Time is genuinely wasted in reviews, and no written standard would tell anybody in advance which documents matter.

dayTitle: What a face is at that distance
title: Twenty-two metres, as an angle
task: Work out the angle a face subtends at the file's distance
scene: Vision scientist Frey lights the reconstruction bay and runs a tape to the twenty-two-metre floor mark. She puts a face at the doorway and asks what its features become at an eye across the rebuilt street.
question: Estimate the angle the gap between a person's eyes subtends at the distance the file records.
takeaway: Doubling the distance halves the angle, and the angle is what the eye has to work with.
why: A face reaches the eye as angles, not metres. Angular size is the feature's size divided by its distance, so every step backward shrinks the usable detail. The eye gap here spans about three milliradians, or ten arc minutes. That can make a face visible as a face. Identity depends on smaller relationships inside that angle. The file's distance is therefore not background description. It sets the scale of the information available before memory enters the problem.
assumes: the eyes of an adult face are about six centimetres apart
an angle in radians is a length divided by a distance
answerText: 0.063 ÷ 22 ≈ 0.0029 radians, about ten arc minutes. The face is visible as a face; the identity-carrying features occupy smaller angles inside it.

estimate.prompt: The case summary puts Cardoza twenty-two metres from the doorway. The gap between the eyes of an adult face is about 0.063 m.
estimate.question: Choose the size of the detail and the distance it was seen from.
estimate.relationship: Angular size θ = s / d, with θ the angle at the eye in radians, s the size of the detail and d the distance to it.
estimate.explanation: About three milliradians, or ten arc minutes. That is enough to see a face as a face in good light, while identity depends on smaller relationships within it. The whole-face width and doorway height are plausible measurements, but neither is the detail this calculation asks about.
estimate.solution: 0.063 ÷ 22 ≈ 0.0029 radians, which is about 10 arc minutes.
givens: The gap between the eyes of an adult face is about 0.063 m
The case summary records a distance of 22 m
labels: 0.063  (m, the gap between the eyes of an adult face)
22  (m, the distance the case summary records)
0.15  (m, the width of a whole face)
1.75  (m, the height of the shop doorway)
6  (s, how long the file says she was watching)

equations.about: angular size — how large a detail is at the eye, in radians
the smallest detail an eye can resolve at a given distance

dayTitle: What a face is at that distance
title: Six seconds, and what they hold
task: Establish how much time there was to take anything in
scene: Memory scientist Ren Okada opens Alma Cardoza's first full account at the doorway paragraph. Six seconds, by her estimate, separate the shout from the man crossing the kerb. The bay clock is set to six.
question: Why does six seconds of viewing not deliver six seconds of face?
takeaway: What is remembered is what was attended to, and attention takes one thing at a time.
why: A scene is not encoded as a complete recording. Attention selects some inputs for deeper processing while other visible inputs receive little. Six seconds contained a shout, a doorway, a moving person, a bag and traffic at the kerb. Each competed for limited attention. Event duration is therefore not the same as face-viewing duration. Later confidence cannot recover which fractions of those six seconds were actually spent processing the face.
assumes: memory is built from what was attended to during an event

choices: Attention has to be divided among competing parts of the scene
The eye needs several seconds in one position before it registers anything at all
Short events are stored briefly and are gone from memory within a few days
Threat makes a witness close her eyes for most of the event without noticing
rebuttals: Recognition takes a fraction of a second, so the delay before anything registers is far shorter than that.
Brief events are often remembered for years, and duration alone does not decide how long a memory lasts.
Eyes stay open under threat, and closing them would leave nothing to explain about the account.

dayTitle: What a face is at that distance
title: Predict it before the forty cards turn
task: Predict the description-only suspect-pick share, run the forty-person check, then spend the measurement to see where the choices actually landed.
scene: Marcus Ilori lays Cardoza's first description beside the six 2019 photographs at the identification bench. Forty mock-witness cards are face down beside them. Nobody holding a card has seen the robbery.
question: What suspect-pick share do you expect from the description alone, and does the measured distribution support a fair six-person array?
takeaway: A procedure can be tested by people who know the description but not the event; where they land measures the array rather than memory.
why: A fair lineup should not point to the suspect through the description alone. Mock witnesses are useful because they never saw the event. They can respond only to the description and the photographs. If one photograph attracts most of them, the array is doing part of the identifying. Cardoza's description is broad, so visual matching alone cannot establish fairness. Measuring where mock witnesses land turns that concern into an empirical property of the procedure.
assumes: a lineup is built to be consistent with the description already given
answerText: Measure the picks by photograph. Twenty-six of forty mock witnesses choose Ward from the description alone, a suspect-pick share of 0.65. That result is far from an even six-way spread and becomes the input to the later functional-size calculation.

choices: Anybody chosen to match it will match it, so matching alone cannot make the array fair
The description should have been withheld from the officer who assembled the photographs
No identification procedure of any kind could have been run within two weeks
Cardoza should have been asked to describe the face in more detail before the array
rebuttals: Withholding it would make things worse, since the assembler needs the description to choose fillers at all.
Two weeks is a workable interval, and the objection here is to the array's construction rather than its timing.
More detail is always welcome, and a witness cannot produce detail that was never encoded on the night.

why_this_format: The old choice states that a broad description cannot guarantee fairness. VERIFY makes the player predict the array consequence, run the same forty-person mock-witness check used later, and pay to measure where the choices actually went.
player_does: lock a predicted suspect-pick proportion before the tally is revealed
run forty mock witnesses who know only Cardoza's description
spend the measurement on the pick distribution rather than merely confirming that all forty completed the task
trap_is_satisfied_by: The source supplies 26 suspect picks among 40 mock witnesses, so truth = 26/40 = 0.65. The authored prediction slider spans 0.20–0.80 and the acceptance ratio is [0.80, 1.20]. Truth lies inside the range; a prediction of 0.80 gives 0.80/0.65 = 1.23 and fails. The one-check measurement budget is invented authoring scaffolding.

data.decision: Does the description-only mock-witness test behave like a fair six-person array?
data.hint: Lock a predicted share before the cards turn. Then run all forty volunteers and spend the one check on the distribution of picks, not just on whether the run completed.

intervention.label: Run 40 mock witnesses from the first description only

failure_feedback.action: spending the check only on completion
failure_feedback.consequence: the run is confirmed but the array's description-driven pull remains unmeasured
failure_feedback.line: Forty people finishing tells me nothing about where the array sent them.

title: Where the sightline goes
task: Find the station where face identification breaks down
scene: Reconstruction technician Bekele has seven distance marks down the bay floor and a face at the far end. Each station card records what twelve volunteers described there and how often they later named the right person from six.
question: The volunteers could describe something from every mark. At which station does naming the individual stop working?
takeaway: Describing a build is not identifying a face, and the two fail at different distances.
why: Large features survive distance longer than identity does. Build, clothing, hair and rough age need only coarse visual information. Identifying one face among similar faces depends on smaller relations between features. Those relations disappear first as angular size shrinks. In the bay, volunteers still describe a person beyond twenty metres while correct naming falls to chance. That distinction matters. A witness can truthfully report seeing a man while the information needed to recognize which man is already gone.
assumes: features can be described without the person being identifiable
the same face was used at every distance
answerText: Naming first falls to chance at the twenty-metre station: two of twelve, which matches blind picking from six. Descriptions of build and clothing still survive there.

title: What the dark takes
task: Establish what the eye gives up in a dark street
scene: Priya Raghunathan shuts the booth door and waits ten minutes. She can then find the chart on the far wall but cannot name its colours. She wanted the room to experience that loss before reading about it.
question: What does a witness lose when a scene is dark enough that only rods are working?
takeaway: Sensitivity in a dark place is bought, and the price is paid in what the eye can no longer separate.
why: Cones provide colour and fine central detail, but they need more light. Rods work when illumination falls and trade detail for sensitivity. They also pool signals across retinal areas, which makes the result coarser. A dark street therefore does not simply dim a face. It removes colour and fine relationships while preserving movement, outline and broad form. That pattern can support confident description of some features while leaving identification detail weak.
assumes: the retina has two kinds of light-sensing cell with different jobs

choices: Colour and fine central detail
Movement, because motion detection needs cone vision
Peripheral vision, because rods disappear there first
Distance judgment, because depth cues require bright light
rebuttals: Motion is detected well in low light; rods are highly sensitive to change.
Rods dominate the periphery, so peripheral detection survives better than fine central detail.
Depth uses several cues and does not disappear simply because cones are no longer carrying colour.

equations.about: illuminance falling off with the square of the distance
sensitivity — telling apart, separated from willingness to choose

title: One claim, or four
task: Take apart the sentence the panel actually hears
scene: Grace Ntuli plays a panel recording in the hall. A volunteer juror repeats 'she saw his face' eleven times across forty minutes. By the end, nobody in the room is asking how far away the face was.
question: Why does the phrase "she saw his face" make a room's decision harder rather than easier?
takeaway: "I saw his face" bundles a distance, a light level, a duration and a recognition into one unarguable sentence.
why: 'She saw his face' bundles several claims into one sentence. It contains distance, illumination, viewing time and recognition. Treating the phrase as one fact forces a reviewer to accept or reject all four together. Separating them is not an attack on honesty. It is how each claim becomes testable. Distance, lighting and timing can be checked without asking the witness again. Recognition is the part that remains tied to memory and procedure.
assumes: a repeated phrase becomes the thing a room is deciding about

choices: It states four separate things at once, so no one of them can be examined
It comes from the witness rather than from an expert, which juries weigh more heavily
It is emotional language, and emotional language dominates a deliberation
It is short, and short statements are recalled better than long ones at the end of a session
rebuttals: Juries do weigh eyewitnesses heavily, and that is about the source of the claim rather than its structure.
The phrase is plain rather than emotional, which is part of why it passes unexamined.
Brevity aids recall, and a longer sentence stating the same bundle would cause the same problem.

dayTitle: Two lamps and a wet road
title: How much light the corner had
task: Work out the illuminance on the doorway from the column
scene: Frey has the column's specification from the utility: a 1,800 candela lantern, twelve metres from the shop doorway along the kerb. The scene report's word for this is "normal".
question: Estimate the illuminance the column put on the doorway when it was working.
takeaway: Illuminance is set by the distance from the lamp to the thing lit, not by the distance to whoever is looking.
why: Light from a source spreads over increasing area, so illuminance falls with the square of distance. The relevant distance runs from the lantern to the doorway it lights. Cardoza's distance belongs in the angular-size calculation instead. A working 1,800-candela lantern at twelve metres gives 12.5 lux. That is dim street lighting, not darkness. The calculation is sound. Whether the lantern was actually on that night is a separate factual question the calculation cannot answer.
assumes: light from a single source spreads over an area that grows with distance
answerText: 1800 ÷ 12² = 12.5 lux if column 4471 is working. That is the modeled lamp contribution, not proof that the lamp was on that night.

estimate.prompt: Column 4471 carries an 1,800 candela lantern and stands twelve metres from the shop doorway. Cardoza was twenty-two metres from the doorway, on the far pavement.
estimate.question: Choose the intensity of the lamp and the distance from it to what it is lighting.
estimate.relationship: Illuminance E = I / d², with E in lux, I the source intensity in candela and d the distance from the source to the lit surface.
estimate.explanation: About 12.5 lux with the lantern working. The twenty-two metres belongs to the observer and therefore to the angle calculation, not this lighting calculation. The arithmetic answers what the lamp would deliver if lit. The utility record later answers whether that premise was true on 14 November.
givens: The column stands 12 m from the shop doorway
labels: 12  (m, from the column to the doorway)

equations.about: illuminance falling off with the square of the distance

dayTitle: Two lamps and a wet road
title: The middle of the event and its edges
task: Which explanation fits all four readings rather than the loudest one?
scene: Priya Raghunathan has four parts of Cardoza's account on the screen. One shows detailed recall, one shows nothing, one is wrong, and one was never mentioned. She wants one mechanism that fits the whole pattern.
takeaway: Arousal does not print or erase a scene; it narrows what is taken in, so the centre is sharp and the edges were never there.
why: Arousal does not strengthen every part of memory equally. Threat narrows attention toward the most urgent object and reduces processing elsewhere. That can produce weapon focus and inattentional blindness in the same event. Cardoza reports many details about the bag and none about the second man. Broad features such as build and jacket remain stable. The pattern is therefore structured rather than globally unreliable. Stress predicts where information may be dense and where it may never have been encoded.
assumes: a threat triggers a fast alarm response before any decision is made
attention narrows under threat

choices: The account is unreliable throughout
Attention narrowed onto the threat
She is filling gaps to be helpful
The interviews were badly conducted
choiceMechanisms: A witness who is wrong about one thing is wrong about everything.
What was attended to is detailed, what was outside it was never encoded, and time is overestimated under arousal.
Details are being invented to satisfy the interviewer.
The questions failed to ask about the second man.
rebuttals: Nothing here is wrong except the duration, and the features that survived are the ones a narrowed account keeps.
Invented detail drifts between tellings, and these three tellings do not drift.
The interviews did ask about the second man; the answer was that she had not looked at him.
text.headline: The account is minutely detailed in one place and empty in others, and both are being read as unreliability.

dayTitle: Two lamps and a wet road
title: A word where a reading should be
task: Decide what the phrase in the scene report is worth
scene: Unit Director Ines Baptiste stands on the rebuilt corner beside the lux meter and the scene report. The report says only 'street lighting normal.' No night reading survives. She asks how much longer Ward should serve while the unit treats that word as data.
question: Why can the review not simply accept "street lighting normal" as evidence about the light?
takeaway: A word describing a condition and a reading of that condition are different kinds of evidence, and only one can be checked.
why: 'Normal' is a judgment against an unstated comparison. It could mean the lamps looked usual, that nothing seemed unusual, or simply that the road was familiar. Those meanings imply different physical conditions. None gives a lux value another reviewer can reproduce. A meter reading carries a defined quantity and unit. Seven years later, somebody else can make the same measurement. A descriptive word cannot supply that missing standard, however sincere the writer was.
assumes: a measurement can be repeated by somebody else and a description cannot

choices: Nobody can now say what the officer compared it against
Officers are not trained to assess lighting conditions at a scene
The report was written the following morning rather than at the scene
A single observer is never enough to establish a physical condition
rebuttals: Training is not the issue, because a trained observer's impression would still lack a stated comparison.
Timing would matter for detail recall, and the phrase would be equally uncheckable written on the spot.
One observer with an instrument is sufficient, which is what shows the problem is the phrase rather than the number of people.

equations.about: illuminance falling off with the square of the distance

title: The order an account is taken in
task: Order the steps of an interview that protects what the witness actually has.
scene: Ren Okada lays five interview steps along the corridor floor and queues the 18 November recording. In the audio, the second question arrives eleven seconds after Cardoza begins. He asks the room to rebuild the order before replaying it.
takeaway: Every question narrows what comes next, so the questions go last and the witness's own account goes first.
why: Interview order protects later information from earlier contamination. First, make 'I do not know' an acceptable answer. Then take uninterrupted free recall before adding anybody else's words. Open questions can follow because they expand material the witness already raised. Closed questions come later and only on existing topics. Confidence must be recorded before photographs or feedback arrive. Once outside information enters, the original state of the account cannot be recreated by asking more carefully.
assumes: a question can introduce a detail that was not in the witness's own account

cards: Say plainly that "I do not know" is a full answer and will not disappoint anybody
Take an uninterrupted account in the witness's own words, asking nothing during it
Return to what the witness raised, using open questions that name no new detail
Put closed questions only about things the witness has already brought up
Record how sure the witness is of each element, before any photographs exist

title: Eleven small agreements
task: Change one feature of the listening room at a time, then reverse the change that moves which details survive into the second telling.
scene: Grace Ntuli plays the 18 November interview in the listening room. Cardoza's husband is present throughout and agrees at eleven points. A second console can replay the same account with one feature of the room changed.
question: Which room feature is causing reinforced details to survive, and does the effect return when that feature is restored?
takeaway: A social effect becomes causal evidence only when the social cue changes and the rest of the room does not.
why: Social feedback can shape an account without anyone intending to coach it. A speaker notices which sentences receive agreement and which receive nothing. Reinforced parts are more likely to be repeated later. Unreinforced parts can shrink or disappear. The mechanism is selective retention, not necessarily invention. A controlled comparison can test it by changing listener reactions while holding the interviewer and timing steady. That separates a room effect from other features of the interview.
assumes: people adjust what they say to the reaction they are getting
answerText: The listener agreement is the causal feature in this authored control run. Eleven agreement cues raise repeated details from 8.0 to 11.0; changing question count or pause length does not. Restoring silence returns the result to 8.1.

choices: Strengthens whatever they respond to and quietly drops the rest
Causes the witness to invent details in order to please them
Makes the witness less willing to admit any uncertainty at all
Slows the account down until detail is lost from the middle of it
rebuttals: Invention is a stronger claim and needs pressure rather than agreement; the ordinary effect is selection.
Willingness to admit doubt does fall in company, and the change here runs through what gets repeated.
The pace of an account is not what agreement changes; what changes is which parts survive.

why_this_format: The old choice names a social-influence mechanism. CONTROL makes the player isolate listener agreement from question count and interviewer pacing, then confirm the effect by reversal. That is stronger AP Psychology practice than recognizing the correct label.
player_does: hold question count and pause length fixed while changing listener agreement
compare the repeated-detail count with repeat noise
restore the listener to silence before naming the causal feature
trap_is_satisfied_by: Invented volunteer-run outcomes because the source gives eleven agreement points but no controlled replication values. The agreement manipulation changes repeated details by 3.0 against 0.7-detail repeat noise, or 4.29× noise, exceeding the required 3× threshold of 2.1. Reversal returns 11.0 to 8.1 near the 8.0 baseline.

data.hint: Change one control from baseline, read the number of details that survive into the second telling, then restore it. Do not change two room features together.

failure_feedback.action: changing agreement cues and question count together
failure_feedback.consequence: a larger second telling can be attributed to either manipulation, so the room effect remains ambiguous
failure_feedback.line: One room, one change. Otherwise you have a story, not a cause.

title: The man may not be here
task: Find the instruction that was not given
scene: Ilori has the 2019 array form. There is a line for the witness's signature and no line for the caution that the person she saw might not be among the photographs. In 2019 there was no such line.
question: What does the missing caution change about the task Cardoza was given?
takeaway: Without being told the offender may be absent, a witness answers "which of these" rather than "is he here".
why: A witness usually assumes police have brought photographs for a reason. Without an explicit caution, 'none of them' can stop feeling like a real answer. The task then shifts toward finding the closest face among the six. An offender-absent lineup still produces a winner under that rule. A may-not-be-present instruction restores rejection as an expected response. It changes the decision criterion before any face is judged, which is why the warning belongs before the array appears.
assumes: a witness expects an investigation to have found somebody before showing an array

choices: It turns the task into choosing, rather than deciding whether to choose
It removes her right to decline to take part in the procedure
It means her choice could not be recorded as a formal identification
It prevents the array from being repeated later with different photographs
rebuttals: Declining was always allowed; what was missing was any statement that not choosing was a real answer.
The choice was recorded and used as an identification, which is the problem rather than a bar to it.
Repeat procedures are ruled out by having seen the first array, not by anything in the caution.

dayTitle: The photograph in the evening paper
title: The scar
task: Which explanation fits every dated item rather than the most damning one?
scene: Ren Okada has four dated items on the screen when Unit Director Ines Baptiste asks whether Cardoza is lying about the scar. Okada says that question arrives too late. He puts the dates across the corridor instead.
takeaway: Post-event information is stored as memory of the event, because memory does not tag what it took in from where.
why: Memory often preserves content better than source. A detail seen in a newspaper can later feel as though it came from the event itself. Source monitoring becomes harder as time and later exposure accumulate. That can produce an honest, confident memory with the wrong origin. The dates matter here. Cardoza's long first interview contains no scar. Ward's photograph appears the next day. The scar enters later. Certainty cannot repair the missing source label.
assumes: a remembered detail carries no label saying where it came from

choices: She is lying about the scar
The detail arrived from the photograph
She saw it and forgot to mention it
The interviewer suggested it in November
choiceMechanisms: The detail was added deliberately to strengthen the identification.
Information met after the event is stored as part of it, and its source is lost first.
A detail can be encoded and left out of an early account.
The word came from the question rather than the witness.
rebuttals: Lying predicts hesitation and inconsistency, and there is none — she is certain, which fits an honest source error better.
A forgotten detail can reappear, and it would not so often be the detail that ran in a photograph the next evening.
The November transcript contains no mention of a scar by anybody, so the suggestion has no route in.
text.headline: A chin scar is absent from the account taken four days after the robbery and present in the statement five weeks later.

dayTitle: The photograph in the evening paper
title: Close the forty-two days
task: Close the chronology from the robbery to the later certainty statement and find the interval the simplified file leaves out.
scene: Tomas Weill lays four dates along the identification corridor: 14 November, 18 November, 19 November and 26 December. The spans almost close. Nell Achterberg has independent records for each date and one missing interval to account for.
question: Where do all forty-two days go, and which missing interval changes what sources were available to the witness?
takeaway: Chronology is only as complete as the intervals it preserves, especially when a missing interval contains a new source of information.
why: Chronology is evidence only when its intervals are independently anchored. The robbery is 14 November. The full interview is four days later, the photograph one day after that, and the array fifteen days later. The later certainty statement follows after another twenty-two days. Those intervals close to forty-two days. Leaving out the one-day newspaper interval creates a gap exactly where new face information entered. Dating does not prove causation, but it defines which sources were available before each account.
assumes: a document's date can be checked against the record of when it was received
answerText: The forty-two days close as 4 + 1 + 15 + 22. The hidden one-day interval is 18 to 19 November, between the first full interview and publication of Ward's photograph.

choices: One predates the photograph and one follows it, with both dates confirmed elsewhere
The two accounts were taken by different officers in different buildings
The November account is longer, so it can be searched for anything the later one adds
The December statement was signed, which makes it the more formal of the two
rebuttals: Different officers would help against interviewer effects and say nothing about when a detail arrived.
Length matters for what could have been said, and an absence in a long account still needs a dated boundary to mean anything.
Formality decides what a document is for, not when the detail inside it first appeared.

why_this_format: The old choice asks why document order matters. BALANCE makes the player close the dated ledger and discover that leaving out one day removes the exact interval in which the newspaper photograph entered after the first full interview.
player_does: count the independently dated spans from 14 November to 26 December
notice that the visible intervals total only forty-one days
add the one-day interview-to-publication interval and identify what entered the record there
trap_is_satisfied_by: All dates are fixed in the source. The visible spans are 4 days from robbery to full interview, 15 from photograph to array, and 22 from array to certainty: 4 + 15 + 22 = 41. The total is 42 days. Adding the hidden 1-day interview-to-photograph span closes the ledger exactly.

total.label: 14 November robbery to 26 December certainty statement

streams.label: First full interview to newspaper photograph
streams.note: The Register publishes Ward's photograph in this interval.

data.hint: Close the days first. The missing term is an interval, not a document. Only after the total reaches forty-two should you ask what entered during that interval.

failure_feedback.action: closing the chronology at forty-one days
failure_feedback.consequence: the only omitted day is the day the newspaper photograph enters between the uncontaminated interview and later procedures
failure_feedback.line: A missing day is still a source opportunity. Put it back.

dayTitle: The photograph in the evening paper
title: What the hormones cannot explain
task: Rule the biology in or out for a change five weeks later
scene: Raghunathan is asked whether the stress of the robbery could have delayed the scar into the account. She draws the time course of the alarm response on the board: seconds, minutes, and hours.
question: Why can the stress response not explain a detail that first appears five weeks after the event?
takeaway: The body's alarm response acts on encoding and on the hours after it, so it cannot account for something that appears weeks later.
why: Stress biology acts during the event and the hours that follow. The amygdala responds rapidly, and cortisol changes over minutes. Those systems can affect attention, encoding and consolidation. They cannot insert a new facial feature five weeks later. The relevant biological window has long closed by then. Stress still matters elsewhere in this case because it can explain uneven encoding across the scene. It does not explain a detail that first appears after later information has entered the record.
assumes: the stress response has a time course that can be measured

choices: It acts during encoding and the hours of consolidation that follow
Stress hormones are cleared within minutes, so later memory is unaffected
Stress changes emotional content only, leaving neutral facial detail untouched
A second stress response in December could rewrite what was encoded in November
rebuttals: Cortisol persists longer than minutes, but the relevant window is still hours rather than five weeks.
Arousal affects attention across the scene; it is not limited to content that feels emotional later.
A December stress response acts on December processing. It cannot insert a feature into November encoding.

title: Agreement is not independence
task: Find the source the agreeing accounts have in common
scene: Five items in the file point the same way. Grace Ntuli has them on the board with their derivations closed. Ines Baptiste asks why the unit is spending a morning on the part of the case nobody disputes.
question: Four of these five point at Ward. Open them, keep whatever still stands on its own, and name the source they have in common.
takeaway: Evidence that agrees because it shares a source carries the weight of one item, not of several.
why: Agreement counts as corroboration only when the sources are independent. Three items here pass through the same newspaper photograph. Their agreement therefore does not create three separate measurements. Remove the shared source and their independence disappears. The till roll and depot camera are different because neither depends on the photograph or on a witness identifying Ward. Those sources can disagree with the case narrative. Evidence earns extra weight when it had a real chance to come out differently.
assumes: two pieces of evidence built on the same source can only ever agree
answerText: The shared source is the Hallam Register photograph. Three Ward-pointing items pass through it, so they are not independent. The till roll and depot camera keep their weight because neither touched that source.

title: Twenty minutes on the kerb
task: Work out what twenty minutes of waiting cost
scene: The first officers arrived at 21:58. Between the robbery and their arrival, Cardoza and Aktaş stood together outside the shop. Okada asks what the file can now say about the four particulars they agree on.
question: What has the wait outside the shop done to the two accounts?
takeaway: Once two witnesses have talked, their accounts cannot be added together, and neither can be recovered alone.
why: Co-witness discussion makes two accounts partly dependent. One person's detail becomes available to the other as content, and later source memory may not preserve where it came from. That means four shared particulars cannot simply be counted twice. The contamination also cannot be subtracted afterwards. Investigators separate witnesses because independence is easiest to protect before accounts meet. Once Cardoza and Deniz Aktaş talked for twenty minutes, agreement stopped being clean evidence that both had encoded the same detail independently.
assumes: people compare accounts when something has just happened to both of them

choices: They are no longer independent accounts
They now cover more of the event because two viewpoints have been combined
They remain independent because both witnesses were describing the same person
Only Aktaş's account is affected because his original view was poorer
rebuttals: Two viewpoints help only when the accounts are collected before they can influence each other.
Describing the same person is the very claim agreement was supposed to support; discussion makes that agreement dependent.
Both accounts can exchange material. A better original view does not protect a witness from later source confusion.

title: Looking out of a lit room
task: Work out what the man behind the counter could see
scene: Bekele has the bay set up from the shop side. The counter, the window, the interior lights at the level the shop record gives. Beyond the glass, the street at the illuminance the corner had.
question: Why is Aktaş's view of the street worse than his position suggests?
takeaway: An eye set for a lit room is the wrong eye for a dark street, and the glass makes it worse.
why: Visual sensitivity adapts to the light level surrounding the eye. A bright shop sets sensitivity too low for a dim street. Dark adaptation can improve that, but it takes minutes. Aktaş did not have those minutes during the robbery. The window creates another problem. Interior light reflects from the glass and overlays the darker scene outside. Distance alone therefore overstates his viewing advantage. A closer witness can still have poorer usable vision when the lighting around the eye is wrong.
assumes: the eye adjusts its sensitivity to the general level of light it is in

choices: His eyes are adapted to the bright shop, and the glass reflects it back
The counter blocks the part of the doorway where a face would appear
Ordinary window glass removes more than half the light from outside
His reflection hides only the centre of the window and leaves the face clear
rebuttals: The counter is low enough that it does not block a face at the doorway.
Ordinary glazing transmits most outside light; reflected interior light is the larger problem here.
A reflection can overlay much of the view when the room behind the observer is brighter than the street.

equations.about: illuminance falling off with the square of the distance
sensitivity — telling apart, separated from willingness to choose

title: Six photographs, and how many alternatives
task: Turn the mock-witness tally into the array's real size
scene: Marcus Ilori spreads forty mock-witness tally marks across the identification bench. Twenty-six sit under one photograph. The volunteers had Cardoza's description and nothing else. He asks how many real alternatives the six-photo array actually offered.
question: Estimate the functional size of the 2019 array.
takeaway: Nominal size is how many faces are on the table; functional size is how many of them a stranger could land on.
why: Lineup protection comes from real alternatives, not from the printed number of photographs. If all six fit the description equally, guessing should spread across them. Mock witnesses test that because they know only the description. Here twenty-six of forty choose Ward's photograph. Functional size is therefore 40 divided by 26, about 1.54. The nominal array had six members. Its effective protection was closer to one and a half alternatives, making an innocent-suspect pick far easier than the form suggests.
assumes: a lineup member who nobody would pick from the description is not an alternative
answerText: 40 ÷ 26 = 1.54 effective members. A nominal six-photo array offered only about one and a half real alternatives to description-only mock witnesses.

estimate.prompt: Forty mock witnesses read Cardoza's description and were shown the 2019 array. Twenty-six of them chose Ward's photograph.
estimate.question: Choose the number of mock witnesses and the number who landed on the suspect.
estimate.relationship: Functional size FS = m / k, with m the mock witnesses asked and k how many of them chose the suspect.
estimate.explanation: About 1.54 effective members. Six photographs were printed, but the mock-witness choices behaved as though only about one and a half were real alternatives. The nominal size and filler count are useful distractors because functional size is designed to test whether those printed numbers overstate the protection.
givens: 40 mock witnesses were shown the array
26 of them chose the suspect from the description alone

equations.about: functional size — how many members of a lineup were real alternatives

title: Moving the middle is not narrowing the spread
task: Bring the procedure inside the fair band
scene: Weill has the mock-witness result as a distribution against the band a fair six-member array would sit in. Four changes are available to the unit's recommendation and each of them costs days of drafting.
question: Bring the recommended procedure inside the fair band, and say when it is defensible.
takeaway: A procedure fails on its spread as often as on its centre, and only one kind of change touches the spread.
why: A fair procedure needs both an acceptable centre and a controlled spread. Better fillers and a may-not-be-present caution can move average performance toward the fair band. They do not remove variation between administrators and rooms. Standard scripts and blind administration reduce that spread. A recommendation should therefore ask how many real administrations remain unfair, not only where the average lands. Moving the centre can improve a mean while leaving too many individual procedures outside the acceptable region.
assumes: a fair six-member array is picked from at about one time in six
a recommendation can propose changes to a procedure as well as criticise it
answerText: Use all four changes. Better fillers and the caution move the centre but still leave too many administrations outside the fair band. Blind sequential presentation and a standard script narrow the spread enough to clear it.

title: A face on paper
task: Work out what a photograph asks the eye to do
scene: Frey has the array photographs and a live volunteer at the same distance under the same lamp. She asks the room which of the two tasks is closer to what Cardoza was doing on 14 November.
question: What does an array of photographs remove from the recognition task?
takeaway: A photograph is one frozen view under somebody else's light, and recognition uses movement and a range of views.
why: Real face recognition draws on changing views. Head turns, expression, gait and feature motion all add information across time. A lineup photograph freezes one angle under one lighting condition. The witness must compare that single view with a memory that was never a still image. That makes the task harder and can make photographs uneven. One person's chosen image may resemble the remembered view more by chance than another person's, even when both are equally plausible fillers.
assumes: a face is recognised from more than a single frozen view of it

choices: Movement and all but one view of the face
Colour, which is the main cue used first in face recognition
Scale, because a smaller printed face is harder to recognise
Context, because the street itself supplies the identity cue
rebuttals: Colour can help, but motion and changing viewpoints are the larger information loss between a live face and one photograph.
Visual recognition handles changes in apparent size routinely; printed scale is not the main loss.
Context is removed too, but that is not the face information a photograph freezes into one view.

title: Where the twenty-two came from
task: Which explanation is consistent with all five items?
scene: Bekele hooks the tape at Cardoza's repeated position and walks past the file's twenty-two-metre floor mark. The tape keeps going to 34.2 m. Tomas Weill puts the unscaled sketch and the shop lease plan beside it.
takeaway: A number that entered a file without a measurement behind it never becomes a measurement by being repeated.
why: The 22-metre figure is the only distance here without a repeatable measurement behind it. Bekele's survey gives 34.2 m, and the lease plan independently matches that geometry within 0.2 m. Cardoza also places herself at the same location across three accounts. The summary traces back to a sketch marked not to scale. Repetition then gave the estimate the appearance of a measured fact. Nothing has to be falsified for a number to acquire false authority through copying.
assumes: a measurement can be repeated and an estimate cannot

choices: The witness has misremembered where she stood
The summary was read off a sketch with no scale
The street has been rebuilt since 2019
The survey is in error
choiceMechanisms: The account of her position is wrong, and the summary is right.
An estimate taken from a drawing became a figure and was then repeated.
The frontage or the kerb has moved.
The measurement was taken from the wrong point.
rebuttals: Her position is the most consistent item in the file and is confirmed by where the launderette stands.
A rebuild would show in the lease plan, which agrees with the survey to twenty centimetres.
A survey error would have to be twelve metres, and the frontage check rules that out independently.
text.headline: The summary and the survey differ by twelve metres, and the street has not changed since 2019.

title: A centimetre of face
task: Work out what an eye can resolve at the surveyed distance
scene: Frey moves the mark to the surveyed distance and reads out the eye's resolution limit in good light. She wants to know what size of detail that limit corresponds to at the far end of the bay.
question: Estimate the smallest detail an eye could resolve at the surveyed distance.
takeaway: The resolution limit is an angle, so the size of the smallest visible detail grows with distance.
why: An angular resolution limit becomes a physical size once distance is supplied. At 34 metres, 0.0003 radians corresponds to about 0.0102 m, roughly one centimetre. Fine facial differences often live at that scale or below. Low light makes the practical limit worse because rod pooling trades resolution for sensitivity. The corrected distance shrinks facial information before lighting is considered. The two-lux scene then removes still more fine detail from the visual signal.
assumes: an eye in good light resolves details about one arc minute across
one arc minute is about 0.0003 radians
answerText: 0.0003 × 34 = 0.0102 m, about one centimetre in good light. Low illumination makes the practical facial-detail limit coarser still.

estimate.prompt: The survey puts the doorway 34 m from where Cardoza stood. An eye in good light resolves about one arc minute, which is 0.0003 radians.
estimate.question: Choose the eye's resolution limit and the distance it is being applied over.
estimate.relationship: Resolution limit s_min = θ_min × d, with θ_min the eye's angular limit and d the distance to the face.
estimate.explanation: About one centimetre in good light. At the corner's two lux, practical resolution is worse. The twenty-two-metre summary figure would give a smaller value, which is why the twelve-metre correction matters. Whole-face spacing and the working-lamp lux value belong to other questions, not this multiplication.
givens: An eye in good light resolves about 0.0003 radians
labels: 12.5  (lux, the corner with the lamp working)

equations.about: the smallest detail an eye can resolve at a given distance
illuminance falling off with the square of the distance

title: What this does and does not settle
task: State what the corrected distance licenses the review to say
scene: Baptiste wants the finding in the report by the end of the week. Ilori asks her to write the sentence first, because the sentence is where reviews are lost, and the room spends an hour on one line.
question: What is the review entitled to conclude from the corrected distance?
takeaway: A measurement can show that a procedure could not support a recognition without showing that the recognition was wrong.
why: These measurements bound the information available to the eye. They do not observe who stood in the doorway. A witness near a visual limit can still identify correctly by chance or by information the reconstruction does not capture. The review therefore cannot infer innocence from poor viewing conditions. It can make a narrower claim about evidence. If the sightline cannot distinguish recognition from a lineup choice, the identification cannot bear more weight than the procedure can support.
assumes: a limit on what could be seen is not evidence about who was there

choices: The sightline cannot establish recognition
Cardoza could not have seen any person leave the shop
Ward could not have been the person in the doorway
The identification would have been reliable at twenty-two metres
rebuttals: The reconstruction shows weak identity information, not an inability to see that a person was present.
Whether Ward was there is a claim about the event, and the sightline cannot answer it.
Even twenty-two metres leaves identification close to the bay's failure range, so the shorter figure would not settle reliability.

equations.about: the smallest detail an eye can resolve at a given distance

title: Change one thing
task: Isolate which feature of the 2019 procedure inflates certainty
scene: The unit's rig runs twenty volunteer administrations at a time. Four features of the 2019 procedure can be switched independently. The readout is reported certainty after a choice, and the room has to isolate which feature moves it.
question: Four features, one effect on certainty. Establish which of them is producing it and prove it.
takeaway: Changing several things at once moves the number and names nothing; one at a time, reversed, names a cause.
why: Several features changed together in the original procedure, so the file alone cannot identify a cause. A controlled test changes one variable while holding the others fixed. If confidence moves, that variable becomes a candidate explanation. Reversing the change is the stronger check. The response should return when the suspected cause is restored. Changing several features together can lower confidence and still leave every causal explanation open. Control and reversal turn association into evidence about which feature actually moved the outcome.
assumes: a feature can only be shown to matter by changing it and changing it back
answerText: Administrator knowledge is the cause in the rig. Removing it drops reported certainty by thirty-one points. Restoring it restores the effect. The other three features move less than the block-to-block variation.

title: Nobody said anything
task: Work out how a belief reaches a witness without being stated
scene: Loomis is clear that she did not point, prompt or name anybody. Ntuli believes her and plays a recording of a volunteer administration where the same thing is true and the effect is visible anyway.
question: How does an administrator's knowledge reach the witness when nothing is said?
takeaway: Expectancy travels through timing and reaction, so an honest administrator transmits a belief as reliably as a dishonest one.
why: Expectancy can leak through behaviour without any deliberate cue. A witness watches pauses, tone, facial reactions and timing because the administrator is the only guide to whether the task is going well. Small differences can therefore carry information. Loomis did not need to point or prompt for knowledge to matter. Blind administration removes the knowledge itself. That is more reliable than asking a well-intentioned administrator to suppress every tiny behaviour that a nervous witness might read as feedback.
assumes: people take up small cues from somebody running a procedure they are taking part in

choices: Through when the pause falls and how the reaction differs between the faces
Through the order the photographs are laid out in, which the witness reads as ranking
Through the administrator's answers to questions the witness asks during the array
Through the paperwork, which names the suspect on a page the witness can see
rebuttals: Layout order does matter and is fixed before the witness arrives, so it cannot carry what the administrator learns during it.
Questions during an array are discouraged and were not asked here, and the effect appears without any.
The array form was face down throughout, and the effect appears in rigs where no paperwork is present at all.

title: What "that's our man" moves
task: Find what confirmation changed besides the confidence
scene: Ren Okada puts the unit's replication on the confidence screen. Half the volunteers are told their choice matched the suspect. Both groups then report how good their original view was and how long they looked.
question: Besides certainty, what does confirming feedback change in a witness's later account?
takeaway: Confirming feedback raises the reported quality of the view itself, which is a report about the past and not a feeling about the present.
why: Post-identification feedback changes more than stated certainty. After being told their choice matches the suspect, witnesses often report a clearer view and longer attention at the event. They can also remember a better position for seeing. Those claims concern the original night but are reconstructed after feedback. That matters in court because 'I had a clear look' sounds like direct evidence about encoding. It may instead partly reflect information learned after the identification was already made.
assumes: a witness reports the conditions of an event from memory, like everything else

choices: Her later report of viewing quality and duration
Her willingness to attend court and repeat the identification
How quickly she made the original choice from the array
How much clothing detail she can report from the event
rebuttals: Feedback can affect willingness to testify, but that is not a reconstructed claim about the original viewing conditions.
The original response time is already fixed on the array record and cannot be changed by later feedback.
Clothing memory can change, but the replicated feedback effect here concerns retrospective reports of viewing quality and attention.

title: Seeing, and being willing to say so
task: Compare the two procedures on how well witnesses told the faces apart
scene: Weill has both procedures' rates on the board. The 2019-style procedure produced more identifications than the blind sequential one, and Baptiste has already called that an argument in its favour.
question: Estimate the sensitivity of the 2019-style procedure.
takeaway: A procedure that produces more identifications may only be producing more of both kinds.
why: A procedure can produce many identifications simply by making witnesses more willing to choose. That raises hits and false alarms together. Sensitivity separates this response tendency from actual discrimination. Converting both rates to standard scores gives a common scale. Here 0.52 minus negative 0.52 gives d-prime = 1.04. The raw rate difference of 0.40 is not comparable in the same way. More choices are not automatically better performance when the extra choices include more false alarms.
assumes: a procedure can be run with the offender present and with the offender absent
a proportion can be converted to a standard score from a table
answerText: d′ = 0.52 − (−0.52) = 1.04. The procedure creates many choices, but its ability to separate offender-present from offender-absent arrays is only modest.

estimate.prompt: In the 2019-style procedure the volunteers picked the offender 70 per cent of the time when he was present, and picked somebody 30 per cent of the time when he was not. The table gives z = 0.52 for 0.70 and z = −0.52 for 0.30.
estimate.question: Choose the two standard scores.
estimate.relationship: Sensitivity d′ = z(H) − z(FA), the hit rate and the false-alarm rate each converted to a standard score and subtracted.
estimate.explanation: About 1.04 standard units of separation. The blind sequential procedure in the same rig reaches 1.9 while producing fewer identifications. Subtracting the raw proportions gives 0.40, but that is not d-prime. Sensitivity uses standardised hit and false-alarm rates so willingness to choose does not masquerade as better discrimination.
labels: 0.70  (the hit rate itself, as a proportion)
0.30  (the false-alarm rate itself, as a proportion)

equations.about: sensitivity — telling apart, separated from willingness to choose
a standard score — one person against the norms

title: Buy the confidence that still means something
task: Spend two authentication credits on the records that determine what Cardoza's confidence can legitimately say about the 4 December choice.
scene: Case analyst Solomon brings four sealed record pulls to the confidence desk. Two can be authenticated before the day's board packet closes. Somewhere in them are Cardoza's words on 4 December and her certainty statement on 26 December.
question: Which records are worth authenticating before the board packet closes?
takeaway: Confidence is evidence about accuracy only when its timing and the information available before it are preserved.
why: Confidence has its strongest relation to accuracy when it is recorded immediately after an uncontaminated identification. Later certainty includes everything learned after the choice. That can include feedback, charging decisions and repeated commitment to the identification. The 4 December form preserves Cardoza's own words: 'maybe, number four.' The 26 December statement says 'absolutely certain.' Both are real records. They answer different questions because three weeks of post-identification experience lie between them.
assumes: a witness's certainty can change between the identification and a later statement
answerText: Authenticate the 4 December array form and the 26 December statement. Together they preserve the change from “maybe, number four” to “absolutely certain” and show why the later wording cannot be substituted for initial confidence.

choices: It was taken before she could learn anything about the choice she had made
It was written by the administrator rather than by the witness herself
It was recorded in the presence of a second officer who countersigned it
It uses a numbered scale rather than the witness's own description
rebuttals: Who held the pen does not decide the value; the timing does, and both documents are properly signed.
A countersignature confirms that a statement was made and says nothing about when the certainty formed.
A numbered scale would help comparison, and a scale applied three weeks late has the same problem.

why_this_format: The old choice can be answered by spotting the earlier date. VALUE makes the player spend scarce record-authentication effort on the two documents whose timing changes the evidentiary meaning of confidence, rather than on adjacent but nondiscriminating records.
player_does: open four possible record pulls and inspect what each could establish
spend no more than two authentication credits
buy the immediate and later confidence records that make the change in certainty visible
trap_is_satisfied_by: Invented two-credit authentication budget; the record contents and dates are source-derived. The four options cost 1 + 1 + 2 + 2 = 6 credits against a budget of 2. The 4 December form and 26 December statement cost 1 each and are both decisive. The options span initial confidence, later confidence, procedure policy and current ability.

data.decision: What can the report legitimately say about confidence at the moment of the 4 December identification?

budget.label: Records that can be authenticated before the board packet closes

data.hint: Buy records whose timing can change the meaning of confidence. A useful adjacent fact can still be poor value for this decision.

options.label: Authenticate the original 4 December array form
options.reveals: The witness's recorded words at the choice were “maybe, number four.”

options.label: Authenticate the 26 December certainty statement
options.reveals: Three weeks later the file records “absolutely certain.”

options.label: Pull the full 2019 array-policy manual
options.reveals: The simultaneous procedure followed the policy of its year; the manual does not recover initial confidence.

options.label: Repeat the 2026 face-matching test
options.reveals: A current matching score says nothing about how certain the 4 December choice was at the moment it was made.

failure_feedback.action: spending both credits on policy and current testing
failure_feedback.consequence: the packet becomes fuller while the change from immediate to later confidence remains unauthenticated
failure_feedback.line: You bought context and lost the two timestamps that change the claim.

title: Column 4471
task: Read what the utility says about the lamp
scene: Vision scientist Frey lays the utility fault ticket for column 4471 beside the bay switch. It runs from 2 to 21 November 2019. She kills the modeled lantern; the doorway meter settles near two lux from shop-window spill.
question: What does the fault ticket do to the twelve lux the review calculated on day four?
takeaway: With the column out, what light the corner had came from a shop window twelve metres the other way.
why: The 12.5-lux calculation described column 4471 if its lantern was working. The utility ticket shows it was out from 2 through 21 November, including the robbery on 14 November. The arithmetic was correct and the premise was false. Bekele's reconstruction leaves about two lux of shop-window spill at the doorway. That is dim rather than dark. It also pushes vision toward rods, where colour disappears and fine facial detail becomes much coarser than in the working-lamp model.
assumes: illuminance falls off with the square of the distance from a source

choices: It removes the source that figure was calculated from, leaving the shop window
It shows the calculation was done with the wrong intensity for that lantern
It means the corner was completely dark, so nothing could have been seen at all
It changes the distance the illuminance should have been calculated over
rebuttals: The lantern's rating is from the utility's own asset record and is not in question.
Two lux is dim rather than dark, and a review that says nothing could be seen overclaims immediately.
The distance from lamp to doorway was correct; the objection is that the lamp was not lit.

equations.about: illuminance falling off with the square of the distance

title: What survives the bad end of nineteen hours
task: Move the cognitive-control assumption to its pessimistic end, then choose the evidentiary treatment that remains defensible.
scene: Priya Raghunathan and clinical psychologist Oyelaran put the custody log beside Ward's 01:20 agreement. Baptiste wants a sentence the board can use. The panel instead asks which treatment of the admission still works if cognitive control was badly degraded.
question: How should the review use Ward's 01:20 agreement if his ability to weigh distant consequences was badly reduced?
takeaway: A decision is more robust when it still works under the pessimistic end of an uncertain psychological state.
why: Sleep loss changes decision control without proving that any statement is false. After nineteen hours awake, immediate relief can outweigh a distant legal cost. Minimisation can strengthen that pressure by making agreement feel cheaper in the room. Ward added no unique detail to the account put to him. He withdrew it after sleep without receiving new information. Those facts make independent corroboration essential. The safest evidentiary use is the one that still works if his cognitive control was near the pessimistic end.
assumes: the ability to weigh a future consequence against a present one degrades without sleep
answerText: Require independent corroboration for any detail Ward supplied himself. At the lowest cognitive-control reserve, this is the only candidate still feasible. It also avoids treating exhaustion as proof that the agreement was false.

choices: He agreed because the account was true
The state and the tactic together
He was intimidated into it
He was confused about the date
choiceMechanisms: The admission reflects what happened on Ferrier Street.
Nineteen hours awake makes ending the interview worth more than the consequence, and an account written for him by the officer needs no knowledge to agree with.
Pressure in the room produced compliance.
A genuine mistake about which evening was being discussed.
rebuttals: A true admission usually brings detail with it, and this one brought none at all.
Intimidation is a different mechanism and the log records no threat; exhaustion and a face-saving account are enough.
He was clear about the date throughout, including in the withdrawal.
text.headline: An agreement given at 01:20 after nineteen hours awake, and withdrawn at 09:30.

why_this_format: The original diagnosis asks for one explanation of the log. STRESS makes the player test possible uses of the admission against uncertainty in cognitive control, so the right move is the one that remains defensible without claiming sleep loss proves truth or falsity.
player_does: move the cognitive-control reserve from nominal to pessimistic
watch evidentiary treatments fail when they require stronger self-control or make unsupported categorical claims
choose the treatment that still demands independent corroboration
trap_is_satisfied_by: Invented robustness scale because the source gives nineteen hours awake but no numeric cognitive-control percentage. At nominal reserve 70, treating the agreement as corroboration has the highest closure score of 100. At pessimistic reserve 20, its feasible threshold of 70 fails. “Corroborate independently” has feasible = 20 and is the only candidate meeting both fixed criteria. The robust candidate is not the nominal closure winner.

data.hint: Move cognitive-control reserve down to twenty. A defensible treatment must avoid treating exhaustion as proof and must not count the agreement as independent knowledge unless Ward supplied new corroborated detail.

criteria.label: Does not count an officer-supplied account as independent knowledge
Does not treat sleep loss itself as proof of truth or falsity

candidates.label: Treat the agreement as independent corroboration
Use only independently corroborated details Ward supplied himself
Discard the agreement solely because he was exhausted
Treat the morning withdrawal as proof the agreement was false

failure_feedback.action: choosing the fastest closure at the nominal setting
failure_feedback.consequence: the conclusion depends on cognitive control being much stronger than the nineteen-hour state allows the review to assume safely
failure_feedback.line: Run your conclusion at the bad end. If it dies there, it was never robust.

title: The cheap version
task: Name what the officer's version of the account offered
scene: Ntuli reads the account that was put to Ward at 01:20. It describes a man who went along with something, who did not plan it, and who was not the one holding the bag.
question: What does offering a lesser version of the act change for somebody in the room?
takeaway: Minimisation lowers what an admission appears to cost, and the law does not price it the way the interview room does.
why: Minimisation changes the apparent price of agreeing. A version where somebody merely went along can feel like an explanation rather than a confession. That makes agreement look like a route out of the room. The legal consequence may remain unchanged. The tactic therefore affects decision framing rather than the truth of the account. It is different from feeding facts, which contaminates content. Here the concern is that the offered story makes immediate compliance feel cheaper than continued resistance.
assumes: people admit more readily to a version that costs them less

choices: It makes agreeing feel cheap while the legal consequence stays the same
It gives the suspect facts he can use to make a false account convincing
It removes the interviewer's obligation to caution him again
It shortens the interview, which is what the tactic exists to do
rebuttals: Feeding facts is a separate fault, contamination rather than minimisation, and it makes an admission look more reliable than it is.
The caution stands throughout an interview and is unaffected by how an account is phrased.
Interviews under minimisation are often longer, and brevity is not what the tactic is for.

title: What Aktaş remembers now
task: Find out what a re-interview after years actually records
scene: Baptiste asks whether the unit should re-interview Cardoza before the report closes. Ren Okada puts Deniz Aktaş's 2023 interview beside his 2019 statement. Four new details appear, each already present somewhere in the public record.
question: What does the 2023 re-interview establish about asking Cardoza again now?
takeaway: An account given years later records everything the person has met since, and there is no way to subtract it.
why: Later interviews cannot be cleaned back to their earlier state. Aktaş's four new details all have sources in the public record, yet he now experiences them as memories of the shop. Good interview technique protects information before contamination. It cannot subtract years of trials, news and retelling. That is why the November 2019 Cardoza account is perishable evidence. Re-interviewing her in 2026 would create another account while destroying the unit's ability to compare future material with an untouched baseline.
assumes: an account can be compared with an earlier account by the same person

choices: A new account would record seven years of exposure rather than the night
A new account would be inadmissible, because too much time has passed
A new account would contain less detail than the original and add nothing
A new account would be reliable if it were taken with a proper interview method
rebuttals: Late accounts are admitted routinely; the objection here is what the account would be evidence of.
New accounts are often longer rather than shorter, and Aktaş's has grown by four details.
Interview method protects an uncontaminated account and does nothing for one that has already met the trial.

title: The pool the identification came from
task: Work out what the identification does to the odds
scene: Weill has two numbers on the board and will not put them together until the room agrees what each of them assumes. One is about Hallam and one is about the procedure.
question: Estimate the odds that the identified man is the offender, given the pool and the procedure.
takeaway: The same identification means one thing in a pool of twelve and another in a pool of four thousand.
why: Evidence changes prior odds by multiplying them. The starting odds depend on the pool of people who could have fit the basic circumstances. The review uses 4,000, giving prior odds of 0.00025. The procedure contributes a likelihood ratio near 15. Multiplying gives 0.00375, about one to 267 in odds. That number depends on both assumptions. The identification is not worthless, but its value cannot be stated without the base rate and the procedure's measured discrimination.
assumes: odds before the evidence are set by how many people could have been responsible
evidence multiplies odds rather than replacing them
answerText: 0.00025 × 15 = 0.00375 posterior odds, about 1:267. The result depends on both the pool assumption and the measured value of the procedure.

estimate.prompt: The review's stated pool is 4,000 men who could have been on that street fitting the description, giving prior odds of 0.00025. The mock-witness work puts the likelihood ratio for an identification from the 2019 procedure at about 15.
estimate.question: Choose the prior odds and the multiplier the procedure earns.
estimate.relationship: Posterior odds = prior odds × likelihood ratio, the odds before the evidence multiplied by how much more often that evidence arises when the claim is true.
estimate.explanation: Posterior odds are 0.00375, about one to 267, on the review's stated assumptions. A stronger procedure would earn a larger likelihood ratio, but the same base rate still matters. The pool size and visual-resolution value are inputs to other parts of the review and are distractors here, not multipliers.
estimate.solution: 0.00025 × 15 ≈ 0.0038, which is odds of about 1 in 270.
givens: Prior odds of 0.00025, from a pool of 4,000
A likelihood ratio of about 15 for the 2019 procedure
labels: 60  (likelihood ratio for a blind sequential procedure)

equations.about: what a match is worth, given who could have been in the pool

title: Six hundred arrays with no offender in them
task: Measure the unit's own procedure against a population it knows the truth about
scene: Ilori has six hundred synthetic cases where the offender is known to be absent, and four versions of the procedure to push them through. What comes back is a measurement of the procedure rather than of anybody's guilt.
question: Run the versions you want, then recommend the one that actually buys something.
takeaway: Running a known population through your own procedure measures the procedure, and the errors it makes are the ones your real cases contain.
why: Every synthetic array here is offender-absent, so every identification is an error by design. The useful question is where those errors land. A filler pick announces itself because the selected person is known not to be the suspect. A suspect pick looks like a normal identification and can travel further through a case. Injection therefore measures the pipeline's blind spot. The best procedure is not the one producing the most identifications. It is the one producing fewer dangerous, non-self-announcing errors.
assumes: a procedure can be run on cases whose answer is already known
when the offender is absent, any pick is an error
answerText: Use blind administration with sequential presentation. It produces the fewest identifications and sends more errors onto fillers, where the mistake is visible. A filler error cannot masquerade as a correct suspect identification.

title: The order the board reads them in
task: Rank three findings by how hard each is to argue with
scene: Three findings sit on one page and the board has ten minutes. Grace Ntuli places the cards along the corridor from the rebuilt corner to the interview room. She asks which finding should make the reader stop first.
question: Which finding should open the report?
takeaway: Put the finding nobody can argue with first, because it is what the arguable ones are then read against.
why: A board gives early claims more attention and uses them to frame what follows. The distance finding is unusually strong because anyone can repeat it with a tape. The lease plan independently confirms it. Opening there forces the reader to confront a concrete error before reaching studies run by the unit. Mock-witness results then explain the procedure. Feedback and custody findings are more inferential. They land better after the report has established that its first reversal is physically repeatable.
assumes: a reader gives most weight to what they read first

choices: The surveyed distance, which anybody can repeat with a tape
The functional size of the array, which rests on the unit's own volunteers
The account of what feedback did to Cardoza's certainty
The custody log's account of the nineteenth hour of interview
rebuttals: The functional size is the review's best experimental work and it is the unit's own volunteers, which is exactly what a sceptical reader questions first.
What feedback did is an inference from a pattern rather than a measurement of this witness, and it reads as speculation in the opening line.
