The custody log is about a different half of the case, and opening on the interview invites the reader to treat the review as advocacy.

title: Three days, and one irreversible purchase
task: Spend the final three workdays on evidence that can still change the report without destroying evidence the unit cannot replace.
scene: Three days remain. Ren Okada lays four proposals on the last empty desk and turns the re-interview card face down. He says one purchase can consume evidence the unit will never be able to restore.
question: Which work do you buy with the last three days?
takeaway: The best evidence purchase changes the decision without consuming information that cannot be recovered later.
why: Evidence has value when it can change the recommendation. The independent survey answers a question the board has already asked and tests the unit's central physical finding. The camera record can settle another dated fact cheaply. More mock witnesses would narrow an interval that is already far from a fair six-person array. Re-interviewing Cardoza is different because it consumes something. It creates new post-event information and ends the possibility of keeping the 2019 account as the last pre-photograph baseline.
assumes: work that cannot change a conclusion is not evidence for it
some evidence is used up by being collected
answerText: Buy the board-appointed independent survey and the 2019 camera-maintenance record. Together they use the three authored workdays and address open physical questions. Do not spend the final window re-interviewing Cardoza or merely tightening the already decisive mock-witness estimate.

proposals: Obtain the 2019 maintenance record for the shop camera, which would date the outage of its own recorder.
Commission an independent survey of the corner by a firm the board appoints.
Re-interview Alma Cardoza with a full cognitive interview.
Extend the mock-witness study from forty volunteers to two hundred.
text.evidence: The unit already holds: Bekele's survey and the lease plan that confirms it; the utility's fault ticket for column 4471; the array form with the witness's words at the time; forty mock witnesses; six hundred known-innocent runs; and the custody log. The board has already asked one question in writing, which is whether the survey was done by anybody independent of the review.

why_this_format: The existing ScienceTank is already close to VALUE. Turning it into the instrument makes the trade-off explicit: the player has three days, four evidence axes, and one option that consumes the uncontaminated comparison rather than merely consuming time.

spend no more than three workdays
fund the independent survey and camera record while leaving the destructive re-interview and extra precision unfunded

The camera record and independent survey are decisive and cost exactly 3 together. The four options span camera chronology, distance provenance, memory and lineup precision.

title: One score, and what it is compared against
task: Read the 2026 test score against the group it should be compared with
scene: Alma Cardoza took a standard face-matching test for the unit in March and scored 42. Tomas Weill opens the age-band norms beside it: mean 51, standard deviation 7, with the rebuilt street visible through the glass.
question: Estimate how far below the norm group's mean Cardoza's score falls, in standard deviations.
takeaway: A standard score says how unusual a result is, which is the only form in which one person's score can be compared with anybody's.
why: A raw score becomes interpretable only against a norm distribution. Cardoza's 42 is nine points below the mean of 51. Dividing that gap by the seven-point standard deviation gives 1.29 standard deviations below the mean. The signed z-score is therefore -1.29. That is low but not a diagnosis. The test was also taken seven years after the robbery. Face matching with pictures present is related to, but different from, identifying a remembered face from a dark street.
assumes: a raw score has no meaning without the distribution it came from
answerText: The score is 1.29 standard deviations below the norm mean; the signed z-score is −1.29. That standardises a 2026 test result and does not recreate 2019 identification accuracy.

estimate.prompt: Cardoza scored 42 on the face-matching test. The norms for her age band give a mean of 51 and a standard deviation of 7.
estimate.question: Choose the norm group's mean, her score and the standard deviation.
estimate.relationship: For a below-mean score, distance below the mean = (μ − X) / σ. The signed standard score is z = (X − μ) / σ, so it has the same magnitude with a negative sign.
estimate.explanation: The score is 1.29 standard deviations below the norm mean, so its signed z-score is −1.29. That locates the score in the norm distribution. It does not diagnose a condition, and it does not recreate vision or memory from 2019. The maximum score and the surveyed street distance are real numbers, but neither belongs in this standardisation calculation.
estimate.solution: (51 − 42) ÷ 7 = 1.29 standard deviations below the mean; the signed z-score is −1.29.
givens: A score of 42 against a norm group mean of 51
A norm group standard deviation of 7

equations.about: sensitivity — telling apart, separated from willingness to choose
a standard score — one person against the norms

title: What being frightened is evidence of
task: Settle what the witness's distress establishes
scene: Oyelaran has been asked twice this week whether Cardoza's distress about the case supports her identification, and once whether it undermines it. He writes both questions on the board and answers neither.
question: What does Cardoza's distress about this case establish about her accuracy?
takeaway: Distress is a real state with no direction in it, and a report that reads it either way has stopped doing measurement.
why: Distress is real and can be measured, but it does not point toward accuracy or error. A witness who was right can be distressed after seven years. A witness who was wrong can be distressed too. Sincerity therefore cannot be converted into identification accuracy. The assessment still has a useful purpose. It can inform whether another interview would harm Cardoza. That is a question about her present welfare, not a way to infer what happened on Ferrier Street in 2019.
assumes: distress can be assessed without assessing what caused it

choices: It establishes distress, not the direction of identification accuracy
It shows the event was encoded more strongly than an ordinary memory
It shows later pressure must have changed the original identification
It proves another interview would be unsafe regardless of her current assessment
rebuttals: Later distress does not measure encoding strength and is separated from the event by seven years.
Years of pressure may affect memory, but distress alone cannot show that it did so in this case.
Whether another interview is safe requires a present clinical assessment. Distress by itself does not settle that decision.

title: What stands behind each sentence
task: Match each claim to what stands behind it.
scene: Four sentences from the draft are on the table. Ntuli asks the room to put each one beside the kind of support it actually has, and warns that one of them has none.
takeaway: Every sentence in a report is answerable in a particular way, and the ones that are not answerable at all should not be in it.
why: Different claims require different kinds of support. A distance can be checked by another survey. A lineup effect can be tested by repeating an experiment. A chronology can be checked against dated records. The claim that Ward was not the man has none of those supports in this review. Leaving that sentence out protects the others. A report gains credibility when each claim has matching evidence. Unsupported conclusions should remain explicitly unresolved.
assumes: claims of different kinds cannot be defended in the same way

choices: Measured on the ground and confirmed against an independent plan.
Measured on strangers who never saw the crime, and repeatable next week.
Established by dates on three documents, none of which is a memory.
Not established by anything in this review, and not what the review is for.
scenarios: The doorway is 34 m from where the witness stood.
The array offered about one and a half real alternatives.
The certainty in the file was recorded three weeks after the choice.
Elias Ward was not the man who came out of the shop.

title: What the board is being asked to do
task: Settle what the recommendation actually asks for
scene: Ines Baptiste has three versions of the closing sentence and has struck out two. Marcus Ilori reads the survivor at the end of the sightline. The board packet closes tonight, after seven years of a fourteen-year sentence.
question: What should the review's recommendation ask the board to do?
takeaway: A recommendation should be no broader than the evidence chain that can still support it under challenge.
why: The review can assess the weight of the identification without reconstructing the robbery itself. Referral asks the body with authority to reopen a conviction to examine evidence that cannot carry the role assigned to it. The same procedural finding also matters beyond Ward because Loomis followed the policy then in force. Discipline would misplace the failure on an individual. An innocence finding would go further than the evidence. The recommendation should match the strongest claim the review can actually support.
assumes: a review recommends a course of action rather than reaching a verdict

choices: Refer the conviction back because the identification cannot carry it alone
Recommend release because the review has disproved the identification
Limit the finding to Ward's case and leave the 2019 procedure out of it
Record the concerns but wait for new evidence about the robbery
rebuttals: The review has shown limits on the identification, not who stood in the doorway.
The procedure is the general finding. Loomis followed the policy then in force, so limiting the result to one case misses the cause.
Waiting leaves a conviction resting on evidence the review has already shown cannot bear the weight assigned to it.

title: What holds if everybody withdraws
task: Name the findings that survive without any witness
scene: Vision scientist Frey shuts the bay lamps down for the last time. She repeats the question from the first morning. Which findings would remain true if nobody involved in the case ever spoke again?
question: Which finding would still stand if every witness in the case withdrew tomorrow?
takeaway: The findings that need no witness are the ones a review can promise will still be there next year.
why: Some findings survive because they do not depend on anyone's memory. Distance can be remeasured. The utility record and reconstruction can establish lighting. Visual limits can be tested again at the same range. Those claims remain available if every witness withdraws. Other findings still matter, but they depend on forms, logs or accounts. Physical measurements are unusually durable because another person can reproduce them later. That makes them the spine of a review that expects its evidence to be challenged.
assumes: a claim about a place can be checked without the people who were there

choices: The distance, the illuminance and what an eye resolves at that range
The certainty recorded on the array form at the time of the choice
The four particulars the two accounts agree on
The state Ward was in at the nineteenth hour of the interview
rebuttals: The array form is a strong document and it is still a record of what one person said.
The agreeing particulars come from two accounts and go with them if either is withdrawn.
The custody log is a record about a person, and its value depends on his account of that night.
